claims.claim_text: An engineering curriculum is zero-sum: the amount of material worth teaching grows every year while the length of the degree does not, so adding anything means removing something else. Processor-level instruction on hardware trainers, worth a semester in the late 1980s, is one of the things that has been displaced.
claims.quote_verbatim: There is just more and more things to learn every year in your engineering degree course
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Catalyzing Change Agents

claims.claim_text: Building a curriculum from first principles upward — starting at what an electron is and working toward circuits — loses students continuously before they reach anything resembling what they came to do.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because they start from, let's learn what an electron is
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Front-loading calculus and physics produces heavy attrition: roughly half of an engineering intake is lost in the first two years.
claims.quote_verbatim: You get 50% fallout just from, just from the math
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: The early theory sequence functions as a weed-out and deters students who arrived interested in electronics but without a background in it; the alternative proposed is to open with a course in which something is built.
claims.quote_verbatim: Why can't you just, you know, build something cool in your first intro class
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Aggravating Agersia Agiotage

claims.claim_text: Teaching material lags practice for structural reasons: writing good course material is a large effort, and institutions buy equipment and then amortise it, so microprocessor courses persisted well after microcontrollers had become the working part.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's really difficult to write good educational course material
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A House of FR4

claims.claim_text: A returning industry engineer evaluating a department found the curriculum unchanged since he had been a student — the same topics, the same designs, the same textbooks — despite a decade of change in what industry needed.
claims.quote_verbatim: things really hadn't changed since I was a student
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Printed circuit design — controlled impedance, spacing, stackups — is absent from many electronics degrees while vector calculus is proved in detail; the answer given by department heads is that students will pick it up over time.
claims.quote_verbatim: in an electronics engineering degree, not even mentioning PCB design or actual circuit design, I find is a bit, bit odd
claims.speaker: Philip Salmony
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: Soldering and the use of laboratory instruments are generally not taught and are assumed to be picked up incidentally; a student whose project work is software-oriented can complete a degree without going near a circuit board and then take a job requiring both.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's so surprising that colleges don't teach soldering or the use of lab instruments
claims.speaker: Leigh Brady
claims.episode_title: Siloed Engineering with Leigh Brady

claims.claim_text: Wholly theoretical programmes exist at well-regarded schools: one electrical engineering degree contained no course in which a student picked up a soldering iron or took a board from schematic to layout, and hands-on work happened only through a laboratory job or a senior project.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is no class at Cornell where you like pick up a soldering iron or design a PCB, like start to finish
claims.speaker: Jeremy Blum
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: Theory earns its place in producing new schemes rather than in daily practice: working out something like frequency modulation required the mathematics first, but once a scheme is understood it can be simplified into a form a practising engineer can use.
claims.quote_verbatim: you often need the complicated theory to work out some of these schemes
claims.speaker: Henry Ott
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Henry Ott - Forced FCC Filtering

claims.claim_text: Education should carry more practical material than it does, and universities generally take the opposite view.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think education should cover more practical stuff, but the universities tend to think otherwise
claims.speaker: Henry Ott
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Henry Ott - Forced FCC Filtering

claims.claim_text: Practising engineers rarely evaluate the integrals taught in the degree; the working method is rules of thumb, with the theory serving as the conceptual base underneath.
claims.quote_verbatim: You need rules of thumb
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Bob Widlar, Electronic Design, FIRST Robotics - Monday, Meta Monday

claims.claim_text: Courses are pitched to the highest level partly so students can discover whether they want to continue into the fields that use it, and so that some of them return to teach it; the number who use that material daily is very small.
claims.quote_verbatim: how they teach to the highest level
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Bob Widlar, Electronic Design, FIRST Robotics - Monday, Meta Monday

claims.claim_text: The teaching aim can be framed as intellectual scaffolding rather than tactics: what matters is the invariants a designer can rely on as technology changes, not the procedure for completing today's design.
claims.quote_verbatim: Think about building your intellectual scaffolding so that you can put other things on top of it as technology inevitably changes
claims.speaker: Tom Lee
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom Lee

claims.claim_text: The order in which theory and practice arrive matters. Coming to the material through math first and then working toward the practical is hard; the students who did best had built things, then knew why they wanted the mathematics. A good instructor has command of the mathematics and knows when not to use it.
claims.quote_verbatim: He had total command of the math, but he knew when and when not to yield this tool
claims.speaker: Tom Lee
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom Lee

claims.claim_text: A hobby background before formal study leaves a body of scattered, half-understood practical knowledge that falls into place when the theory arrives, and supplies the motivation to care about it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had a decade of this hobby experience, just, you know, reading and memorizing all this stuff, which I didn't really understand at the time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Design For Longevity

claims.claim_text: Students do not converge on one explanation: some grasp an operational amplifier from the intuitive model — that the difference between the inputs is zero and everything follows from there — and others need the equations written out before it makes sense.
claims.quote_verbatim: there were students who just didn't grasp it that way. They wanted to have the equations written out for them
claims.speaker: Remco Stoutjesdijk
claims.episode_title: High End Audio with Remco Stoutjesdijk

claims.claim_text: The first two years select for the mathematically inclined, while the students who were repairing electronics at twelve often find them hardest and drop out — a loss of exactly the people the field needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: the mathematics types, they have a very easy first two years in uni
claims.speaker: Remco Stoutjesdijk
claims.episode_title: High End Audio with Remco Stoutjesdijk

claims.claim_text: A course advertised as practically oriented can still be paced for a non-technical intake: a student arriving from a vocational school where he had already repaired radios and designed op-amp circuits sat through a first year that began at Ohm's law and was still on diodes by mid-year.
claims.quote_verbatim: here's lesson number one, Ohm's law. Start from the beginning.
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: A project-per-week course structure teaches a topic and then requires a working artefact using those parts: analogue switches followed by building a function generator, or a motor whose speed is regulated from an encoder input, one week each, in an analogue and mixed-signal course for juniors and seniors.
claims.quote_verbatim: the project of the week will be make a function generator or make a motor that regulates its speed with an encoder input
claims.speaker: Larry Sears
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: Teaching laboratories are deliberately better equipped than the workplaces students will enter; the point is not that they will see that equipment on the job but that it introduces them to how the work is done.
claims.quote_verbatim: They probably won't see that equipment when they go out to get a job
claims.speaker: Larry Sears
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: One grading scheme ties the mark to iteration rather than to a finished result: one prototype earns a D, two a C, three a B, four an A, on the principle that demonstrated progress is what is being assessed.
claims.quote_verbatim: you do one prototype, you get a D. You do two prototypes, you get a C.
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: A complementary scheme caps the required projects at a middling grade and awards the rest for something the student conceives themselves, with no guidance because nobody has done it before. It is slow and difficult to assess, and it is what instils the tenacity the assessment is really after.
claims.quote_verbatim: the more of you you put into whatever it is, the more credit you're going to get
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Teaching reasoning requires problems whose success or failure is evident to the student as well as the instructor; an essay cannot be marked down for insufficient thinking in a way the student can act on.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to do is give them a meaningful problem where success and lack of success is evident to them
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Frequent low-stakes assignments serve as attendance and engagement instrumentation as much as assessment: they take minutes, they show the student their marks accumulating, and they let the instructor see in the grade book which students are fading and reach out before they are lost.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can look at your grade book and online and just see the students that are starting to fade away
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: Distributing notes in advance and recording lectures changes what a lecture is for: an hour spent transcribing equations leaves very little taken in, and a recording that can be paused removes the pressure to keep up in real time.
claims.quote_verbatim: You write frantically for an hour and you have equations
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: A class taught by someone from industry hones in on how the theory is actually used in one company's work, and in particular on CAD tools — how they process information and what assumptions they make — which is how engineering is actually done and is not conveyed by paper-and-pencil theory.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you have somebody from industry teach a class, uh, they hone in on the way that the, they use that theory
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: The standard objection to teaching with industrial tools is that the tools will become outmoded.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can't teach using tools. They might become outmoded
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: Tool choice in teaching is an employability decision: a free design flow lacks process design kits for smaller nodes and is not what industry uses, so students are taught the commercial tool even where the free one is a good tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: someone that's trying to educate students and make them marketable and attractive to potential employers is they don't use electric in industry
claims.speaker: Jake Baker
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jake Baker

claims.claim_text: Higher-level frameworks — a Python interface to FPGA hardware, for instance — are used heavily in teaching because they lower the barrier to entry, where a twelve-week course cannot start at the transistor and build to a Linux system on custom hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: they use it a lot for education just cause it makes it, it kind of lowers that barrier to entry
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: Silicon can be designed with education as a stated purpose: a microcontroller's RISC-V cores were included largely for their educational value, both for users of the chip and for the design team learning to implement a new architecture inside a familiar system.
claims.quote_verbatim: they are mostly valuable on this chip for education
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: One engineering-only college treats its own students as the experiment: the institution's principal research output is attempts at new ways to educate engineers.
claims.quote_verbatim: the main research output of the university is attempts at figuring out new ways to educate engineers
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: That faculty was assembled from local engineering colleges and from people specifically interested in researching how others learn, rather than from a single disciplinary pipeline.
claims.quote_verbatim: just like-minded people that were interested in researching how other people learn
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: A one-credit seminar covering product safety — the regulatory process, what a hipot test is as distinct from an ESD test, why one grounds — is the kind of course that conventional programmes do not contain at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: What it means to do a high pot test versus a ESD test. Why you would want to ground.
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: A summer engineering programme for school students lets each student choose their own project and runs at a three or four to one student-to-staff ratio, which is necessary precisely because the staff have not built those projects themselves and are working them out alongside the student.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have a, like a three or four to one student to staff ratio
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Rebuilding Projects with Dave Young

claims.claim_text: The programme's design target is the experience of having made something work: students are at a soldering iron within an hour of arriving on the first day, choosing from about 130 projects or designing their own, and spending the following six weeks doing whatever it takes to make it work.
claims.quote_verbatim: within an hour of them showing up, they're in front of a solder and working
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: The rationale is that showing school students the joy of creating something new changes what they choose to do with their free time, which is what actually determines whether they enter the field.
claims.quote_verbatim: let's show high school students basically the light at the end of the tunnel, which is the joy of creating something new
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: British apprentice schemes take students directly from school and train them for three years in soldering, board assembly, mechanical assembly and machining. Some become technicians; some go on to engineering degrees, and an engineer who came up that way — hands first, theory afterwards — is among the most valuable, because they carry the reference points for why a one-millimetre plastic sidewall or an unmachinable part is a mistake.
claims.quote_verbatim: an apprentice scheme where they would take in not graduate students from university, but students straight from high school
claims.speaker: Leigh Brady
claims.episode_title: Siloed Engineering with Leigh Brady

claims.claim_text: Not every engineer needs a doctorate. If the definition of the work is taking knowledge from the scientists and creating and maintaining systems that benefit society, vocational training reaches it; the objective is more routes in — a two-year degree, a one-year certificate — rather than one education fitted to everybody.
claims.quote_verbatim: we take knowledge from the scientists and we create and maintain systems that benefit society
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: A two-year technician programme staffed by instructors holding master's degrees in physics, electrical engineering and mathematics delivered analysis and critical thinking alongside the practical qualification, which carried through into subsequent degree study.
claims.quote_verbatim: those guys really put that knowledge of analysis and thinking critically while I was getting the two-year degree
claims.speaker: Don Wilcher
claims.episode_title: Engineering Education with Dr Don Wilcher

claims.claim_text: Ladder logic taught on classroom trainers with pneumatic cylinders and variable-speed drives did not click until it was seen running on a plant floor, where the physical motion and the sound of things going right and wrong supplied the feedback the trainer could not.
claims.quote_verbatim: it clicked when I actually got into industry
claims.speaker: Don Wilcher
claims.episode_title: Engineering Education with Dr Don Wilcher

claims.claim_text: A co-operative education placement adds a semester or so to a degree but supplies both a large correction to how much the student actually knows and paid work; the four-year length of a degree is itself arbitrary.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it was a five-year program instead of four, but like four is so arbitrary anyways
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Doomed To The Flatland

claims.claim_text: Access to engineering study is not uniform: asylum seekers in the United Kingdom were unable to enter engineering courses for about six years, and a campaign directed at vice chancellors and parliament secured equal access at more than seventy-five universities.
claims.quote_verbatim: being an asylum seeker meant that I couldn't access engineering for many, many, many years
claims.speaker: Shrouk El Attar
claims.episode_title: Creative Engineering with Shrouk El-Attar

claims.claim_text: The vocabulary barrier can be more fundamental than not knowing what to search for: sign languages developed without words for resistors and the rest of the electronics vocabulary, so a deaf engineering student and instructor face a gap in the shared language itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: There just aren't words in that language
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Once Every Couple Months

claims.claim_text: It is treated as a basic fact of the industry that a graduate emerges with a foundation and essentially no ability to do practical work, which is why companies need their own training programmes.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you come out of college, you know nothing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Chuck Peddle - Charismatic Chipmaking Coryphaeus

claims.claim_text: What a degree should leave a graduate with is the tools to go and learn, plus enough confidence to believe they can do a thing — a belief that will be wrong many times and remains useful.
claims.quote_verbatim: you should have enough tools to go out and learn
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Todd Bailey - Embedded Embrasure Engineering

claims.claim_text: On-the-job training has thinned because companies decided to rely on schools to provide it, even though what schools provide is the theoretical side.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's not as much on-the-job training experience as there used to be
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: SpaceX, Enclosures & Startups - Urging Unemployment Ullagone

claims.claim_text: Recruiting for applications and systems work is done by hiring from industry and by seating people who have the basic skills next to people with practical experience so they learn from them; what a degree supplies is the ability to learn the practical material afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have the people who have the basic skills and you sit and let them learn from the people who have more practical experience
claims.speaker: Hank Zumbahlen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Hank Zumbahlen - Zoppa Zumbahlen Zateticism

claims.claim_text: A first job that requires error and power budgets across all parts teaches something a build-it-and-see approach does not: how to know in advance whether the design will meet its specification over the whole population, rather than assuming that because the first one worked the thousandth will.
claims.quote_verbatim: I understood how to know if your thing works or not way better after air budget
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Trade-off balancing — more power means more heat, less power means a more expensive part — is central to the work and is not exercised by recipe-style laboratory classes, only by project work where the design is genuinely open.
claims.quote_verbatim: engineering is the art of building something with stuff you can get
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Loopback

claims.claim_text: The engineers who did best were not distinguished by their grasp of physics but by building relationships with field applications engineers and salespeople, getting early information, navigating meetings and constructing project schedules — none of which universities teach well.
claims.quote_verbatim: some of the better engineers I knew were the ones who were like, were building engine, building relationships with like FAEs and salespeople
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Design For Longevity

claims.claim_text: Hands-on time with an instrument builds mental models that theoretical treatment does not: watching a spectrum change as something is varied converts an abstract topic into something that can be visualised and reasoned about.
claims.quote_verbatim: having hands on with the test equipment and like seeing what happens as you change things
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Just Add Salt

claims.claim_text: Being able to build things does not make someone a strong academic engineer, and the gap between solving equations in an examination and working in the field persists in both directions.
claims.quote_verbatim: school won't teach you everything that you need to know to like build things practically
claims.speaker: Aaed Musa
claims.episode_title: Robots Everywhere with Aaed Musa

claims.claim_text: The division of labour between school and job is that school builds the model of how a processor works and why the constraints led the hardware to evolve as it did, and the specific numbers — a three-cycle cache budget, say — are learned on the job while trying to build one.
claims.quote_verbatim: you build the foundations through school. You model your brain.
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Students are trained to ask questions in order to be given the answer rather than out of inquisitiveness, so part of the teaching task is pushing them to work it out themselves.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to encourage students to go figure it out on their own
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: Asking what project to work on is asking someone else to do part of the work: choosing the problem is the skill, and years of being handed assignments is what leaves people unable to choose one.
claims.quote_verbatim: everyone needs to know what they want to work on
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Freelance PCB Design with Petr Dvorak

claims.claim_text: Intimidating concepts — real-time operating system primitives, machine learning — are best approached against a problem the learner actually has; read cold, without a use case, they do not stick.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to scratch an actual itch
claims.speaker: Benjamin Cabe
claims.episode_title: Benjamin Cabé Nose Zephyr

claims.claim_text: Beginner programmes and bootcamps are stepping stones rather than substitutes: they get someone past the point of self-motivation, and real engineering is learned on the job, from a course, a bootcamp or a degree alike.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's about getting equipped with the tools even college you know you're not going to be learning real you learn real engineering on the job
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Glass and Gongkai GSM - Unzymotic Ursidae Upbuilding

claims.claim_text: Beginner classes convert into project work far less often than expected: after running beginner classes and open build sessions at one fabrication laboratory, the overlap ran the opposite way — people came to the open sessions first and then took the classes.
claims.quote_verbatim: The overlap between the classes and the open house events actually ran the opposite direction
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Finishing Prototypes with Zack Freedman

claims.claim_text: One course opens not with technical content but with mindset: what approach the student is going to take when something is not working, since nothing about the subject is easy or simple.
claims.quote_verbatim: I actually start the course right now with, uh, talking about mindset
claims.speaker: Michael
claims.episode_title: Eating An Elephant

claims.claim_text: Teaching well requires re-entering the beginner state, and the part hardest to reconstruct is not the missing knowledge but the feeling of not knowing where to turn or what to search for; writing down what one struggled with at the time does not fully preserve it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't know what to Google for
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Keyzermas Vacation

claims.claim_text: Teaching a subject is how one comes to know it: an instructor drafted to cover a computer architecture course had done poorly in that course as an undergraduate and knew it backwards by the time the semester ended.
claims.quote_verbatim: I knew it backwards and forwards by the time I finished teaching it
claims.speaker: Vic Aprea
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vic Aprea - Federated Firmware Functionalism

claims.claim_text: Students are generally unaware that at a research university the professor's primary job is research rather than teaching, which explains a great deal about availability that is otherwise read as indifference.
claims.quote_verbatim: my primary job is research, not actually to teach you
claims.speaker: Jonathan Ellis
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Ellis

claims.claim_text: An instructor who teaches half time and consults the rest brings the practice into the classroom — build the hardware, make it work, and do the theory and the analysis as well — an approach some faculty look down on.
claims.quote_verbatim: let's build hardware. Let's make stuff work. We'll, we'll, you know, we'll do the theory.
claims.speaker: Kent Lundberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Kent Lundberg - Luculent Linear Legacy

claims.claim_text: Students who do not yet know that something is impossible generate ideas that more often than not turn out to be achievable, where someone with years in industry would have been hardened out of proposing them.
claims.quote_verbatim: being connected with the students that didn't know they couldn't do something
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: A modern class is interactive in a way earlier ones were not: a room of students with computers pushes back on points and checks claims during the lecture, which requires the instructor to know the material rather than deliver it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll be pushing back on certain points or asking these great questions
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: One programme addressed the gap between analytic problem sets and practical building by creating an opt-in elective track of courses built around practical skill building, testing and analysis. It became popular because it makes students feel competent to advertise themselves as engineers and to execute what a team asks of them.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's very based on practical skill building, practical testing, analysis, building that confidence
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: A demanding practical course becomes a hiring signal that industry recognises, and the recognition attaches to the accomplishment in the application space rather than to having completed the problem sets.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not like the, oh, you filled out all the problem sets
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: The signal is strong enough to hire on directly: a candidate who took a particular demanding project course, struggled with it and enjoyed it, is hireable on that basis alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: You take that class. You pass it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Melbourne, Hackerspace & Calibration - Vacuuous Vortex Verification

claims.claim_text: Candidates who can describe only the class project everyone else also did are indistinguishable at a recruiting event; anything outside the required curriculum — a co-op placement, a project of one's own — is what differentiates a graduate.
claims.quote_verbatim: everyone's like so people that haven't done internships or haven't done anything else outside
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Jobs For Weirdos

claims.claim_text: Short courses on a résumé show that someone is proactive about learning, but count for very little once there is experience to look at instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: it shows that you're, you know, you're actually, actually proactive and learning stuff on your own
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Design For Longevity

claims.claim_text: Small undergraduate engineering colleges function as concentrated recruiting grounds, and regional employers claim their graduates early, which is why their alumni are numerous in one industrial region and unfamiliar elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think a lot of the industrial Midwest companies are like, nope, dibs
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: The material a designer most needs and is least likely to have been taught is basic electromagnetic compatibility and the mental models of how electricity actually moves. Vendors have progressively taken over that education because they need engineers capable of using their products.
claims.quote_verbatim: the corporate world has been doing a great job over the past approximately a decade of stepping up
claims.speaker: Zachariah Peterson
claims.episode_title: Layout Review with Zachariah Peterson

claims.claim_text: Regional practice differs in what engineering is for: in several Asian countries engineering is treated as a step to management, and remaining an engineer after ten years is read as a failure rather than as expertise.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're an engineer in 10 years, you're a failure
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: Educational emphasis differs too: teaching in Asia was observed to be more practical, with less of the theoretical basis, while European students would openly challenge an error deliberately planted in an equation where American audiences did not.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it's more practical, you know, learn, see in 15 minutes or whatever it might be with less of the theoretical basis
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: Where students live shapes how universities compete: in Australia students typically stay at home or nearby and choose among the universities in their city, rather than moving across the country to a school chosen for its reputation.
claims.quote_verbatim: you make your choice based on, not necessarily the nearest
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Autorouter, Datasheets & Obscure Chips - Cloddish Collegiate Conversations

claims.claim_text: The Australian accreditation body encourages, without compelling, all universities to cover the same base material, so engineering courses there are fairly similar to one another.
claims.quote_verbatim: they try and make the courses all very similar

claims.episode_title: Autorouter, Datasheets & Obscure Chips - Cloddish Collegiate Conversations
